query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, increasing the Al content increases atomic size mismatch and enhances the ordering enthalpy such that, at lower temperatures, the enthalpic drive overcomes configurational entropy stabilization, leading to the formation of a dual-phase microstructure. At sufficiently high temperatures, high mixing entropy re-stabilizes the single-phase structure, preserving high-temperature strength and environmental resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA with a baseline (low) Al content (e.g., ~10 at% Al) exhibiting a single-phase solid-solution structure.
generation.intervention: Systematically increase the Al content (e.g., from ~10 at% to ~20 at% and ~30 at% Al) while keeping the other elemental ratios constant.
generation.conditions: Samples are processed under identical synthesis and annealing conditions. They are tested under isothermal holds at room temperature, in cryogenic environments, and during high-temperature annealing to assess phase stability and mechanical properties.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion and local compositional fluctuations induced by the increased atomic size mismatch, which promote the nucleation of second phases at lower temperatures.
generation.mechanism: Greater Al content increases the mismatch in atomic radii and alters the electronic interactions, thereby increasing the ordering enthalpy. At low temperatures, this energetic drive overcomes the entropy gain from random mixing, leading to phase separation (dual-phase formation). At high temperatures, however, the enhanced configurational entropy counters the ordering enthalpy, thus maintaining the single-phase structure essential for environmental resistance and high-temperature strength. This competition also correlates with changes in deformation mechanisms that govern cryogenic toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline low-Al alloy, alloys with higher Al content will show evidence of phase separation into dual-phase microstructures at room and cryogenic temperatures, which will be associated with a reduction in cryogenic toughness. Under high-temperature conditions, however, the dual-phase nature is suppressed, and a single-phase solid solution is recovered, preserving high-temperature strength and environmental resistance.
generation.baseline: The low-Al (~10 at%) Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy that retains a stable single-phase structure across the temperature range, delivering balanced high-temperature and cryogenic properties.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies only within the compositional limits of the Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni system and for the temperature ranges studied. The specific threshold of Al content needed to trigger phase separation may be sensitive to processing conditions and could vary outside the tested ranges.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship between Al content, the onset temperature of phase separation, and the subsequent changes in mechanical properties remains to be precisely determined. Additionally, processing variations may introduce uncertainties in the critical Al threshold.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys with varying Al contents (e.g., 10 at%, 20 at%, and 30 at%) under identical synthesis and thermal processing conditions. Perform controlled thermal treatments at room temperature, cryogenic temperatures, and elevated temperatures. Analyze the phase structures using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and electron microscopy. Concurrently, measure mechanical properties such as tensile strength, yield strength, and toughness at the corresponding temperatures.
measurements: Phase identification and quantification via XRD
Mechanical properties (tensile tests, toughness measurements) at cryogenic and high temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the Al content does not correlate with the predicted onset of dual-phase formation at lower temperatures (or if the mechanical property trends do not follow the proposed decrease in cryogenic toughness or recovery of high-temperature strength), then the hypothesis is falsified.

They have attracted increasing attention, especially as structural materials, due to their remarkable mechanical strength and resistance to oxidation and fatigue at ambient and elevated temperatures. The compositional complexity does not automatically imply microstructural complexity due to the high mixing entropy. Often, an operational definition for HEAs is a solid-solution phase stabilized by the higher configurational entropy that increases with increasing temperature. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), which were originally developed as concentrated solid solutions of multiple principal elements in equal, or near equal, atomic ratios, have drawn progressively increasing attention over the past decade. Unlike single principal-element alloys, their complex alloy compositions and elemental distribution, together with crystal lattice distortion induced by atomic-size mismatch (depending upon relative atomic sizes), can have a significant effect on the activity of their crystal defects and hence mechanical properties. Although HEAs were initially designed to benefit from single-phase stabilization,, single-phase HEAs are actually not that common, and of those that do exist, only a few display excellent damage-tolerance in the form of combinations of high strength, ductility, and toughness. The well-studied equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi Cantor alloy and its derivatives, in particular the CrCoNi alloy, show exceptional damage-tolerance which progressively improves at cryogenic temperatures, although even these alloys do not have yield (as opposed to ultimate tensile) strengths that are comparable to some advanced steels.
